--- title: "Session 16 — Capstone: The End-to-End Project" subtitle: "The whole pipeline · Market basket analysis · Statistical testing · Advanced models · Delivering it" --- ::: {.callout-note} **This chapter puts all fifteen previous chapters into one project.** **Assumed knowledge:** everything. This chapter introduces exactly one new technique — association rule mining — and otherwise assembles what you already have. **The one idea to take away:** a finished project is not a model with a good score. It is a **question, an honest answer, and a statement of what the answer cannot support.** The last part is what separates a project from a demonstration. ::: ## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s16-outcomes} By the end of this chapter you can: 1. Run a complete project from raw data to a deployable model. 2. Compute support, confidence and lift by hand, and mine rules with Apriori. 3. Read an association rule critically and reject a useless one. 4. Support a claim with a statistical test, not just a chart. 5. Compare several models honestly against a baseline. 6. Write up a project so somebody else can reproduce and challenge it. ## How this chapter is organised {#sec-s16-organisation} | Part | Question it answers | |---|---| | [A — The whole pipeline](#sec-s16-a) | *What does all sixteen chapters look like in one run?* | | [B — Market basket analysis](#sec-s16-b) | *What is bought together?* | | [C — Making claims stand up](#sec-s16-c) | *How do I know my finding is real?* | | [D — Delivering it](#sec-s16-d) | *What do I actually hand over?* | # Part A — The whole pipeline {#sec-s16-a} ## 1. The project checklist {#sec-s16-topic-1} **Before writing any code, answer four questions.** A project that skips this stage usually produces a model nobody can use. | Question | A bad answer | A good answer | |---|---|---| | **What decision changes?** | "we want to understand customers" | "we decide who gets the retention offer" | | **What does success look like?** | "high accuracy" | "catch 60% of churners while contacting under 20% of customers" | | **What data exists, and when?** | "we have lots of data" | "12 months of transactions, available the day after" | | **What would make it useless?** | — | "if it needs data we only have *after* the customer leaves" | ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Fix the success criterion before you model"} Choosing the target metric *after* seeing the results means choosing the metric your model happens to do well on. **Write the number down first**, and keep it visible. ::: ### Demo 1 — the dataset, and the question ::: {#373eb01c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/telecom_churn.csv") print(f"rows: {len(customers):,} churn rate: {customers['churned'].mean():.1%}") print(f"\nQUESTION : which customers will churn in the next quarter?") print(f"DECISION : who receives a retention offer") print(f"SUCCESS : catch 60% of churners (recall ≥ 0.60) while contacting") print(f" fewer than 30% of all customers") print(f"BASELINE : contacting everyone catches 100% but contacts 100%") customers.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rows: 3,060 churn rate: 9.8% QUESTION : which customers will churn in the next quarter? DECISION : who receives a retention offer SUCCESS : catch 60% of churners (recall ≥ 0.60) while contacting fewer than 30% of all customers BASELINE : contacting everyone catches 100% but contacts 100% ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

Steps 1–3: clean, explore, prepare {#sec-s16-topic-2} ### Demo 2 — cleaning, with a report (Session 3) ::: {#f7c3253c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd def clean(df): report, d = {}, df.copy() report["rows_in"] = len(d) d = d.drop_duplicates() report["duplicates_removed"] = report["rows_in"] - len(d) bad = d["tenure_months"] < 0 # impossible before missing report["impossible_values"] = int(bad.sum()) d.loc[bad, "tenure_months"] = np.nan report["blanks_before"] = int(d[["monthly_spend", "tenure_months"]].isna().sum().sum()) d["spend_was_missing"] = d["monthly_spend"].isna() d["monthly_spend"] = d["monthly_spend"].fillna(d["monthly_spend"].median()) d["tenure_months"] = d["tenure_months"].fillna(d["tenure_months"].median()) q1, q3 = d["monthly_spend"].quantile([.25, .75]) report["outliers_flagged"] = int((d["monthly_spend"] > q3 + 1.5*(q3-q1)).sum()) report["rows_out"] = len(d) report["blanks_after"] = int(d.isna().sum().sum()) return d, report clean_df, report = clean(customers) print("CLEANING REPORT") for k, v in report.items(): print(f" {k.replace('_',' '):<22} {v}") print("\nOutliers were flagged, not removed — high spenders are real customers.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CLEANING REPORT rows in 3060 duplicates removed 60 impossible values 40 blanks before 160 outliers flagged 78 rows out 3000 blanks after 0 Outliers were flagged, not removed — high spenders are real customers. ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 3 — exploring, and forming a hypothesis (Sessions 7–8) ::: {#cell-fig-s16-eda .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.2)) sns.boxplot(data=clean_df, x="churned", y="support_calls", ax=ax[0]) ax[0].set_title("Support calls") sns.boxplot(data=clean_df, x="churned", y="tenure_months", ax=ax[1]) ax[1].set_title("Tenure (months)") sns.boxplot(data=clean_df, x="churned", y="monthly_spend", ax=ax[2]) ax[2].set_title("Monthly spend") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("Churn rate by plan:") print((clean_df.groupby("plan")["churned"].agg(["mean", "size"]) .rename(columns={"mean": "churn_rate", "size": "customers"}) .assign(churn_rate=lambda d: (d["churn_rate"]*100).round(1)).to_string())) print("\nCorrelation with churn:") print(clean_df[["tenure_months","monthly_spend","support_calls","churned"]] .corr()["churned"].drop("churned").round(3).to_string()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Churn against each candidate driver. Support calls and tenure separate the groups; spend does not.](session-16-open-ended-module-implementation-and-capstone_files/figure-html/fig-s16-eda-output-1.png){#fig-s16-eda width=1419 height=341} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Churn rate by plan: churn_rate customers plan basic 13.5 1301 premium 6.3 619 standard 7.1 1080 Correlation with churn: tenure_months -0.168 monthly_spend -0.018 support_calls 0.174 ``` ::: ::: **Three hypotheses, formed from the pictures:** support calls raise churn, tenure lowers it, spend does little. Part C tests them properly rather than trusting the eye. ### Demo 4 — preparing, with a pipeline (Session 5) ::: {#0169916b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder features = ["tenure_months", "monthly_spend", "support_calls", "city", "plan"] X = clean_df[features] y = clean_df["churned"] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y) prepare = ColumnTransformer([ ("num", StandardScaler(), ["tenure_months", "monthly_spend", "support_calls"]), ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["city", "plan"]), ]) print(f"train {len(X_train):,} rows test {len(X_test):,} rows") print(f"churn rate — train {y_train.mean():.1%}, test {y_test.mean():.1%} (kept equal by stratify)") print(f"columns after preparation: {prepare.fit_transform(X_train).shape[1]}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` train 2,250 rows test 750 rows churn rate — train 9.7%, test 9.7% (kept equal by stratify) columns after preparation: 10 ``` ::: ::: ## 3. Steps 4–5: model and evaluate {#sec-s16-topic-3} ### Demo 5 — four models against a baseline (Sessions 9–11) ::: {#6c572a01 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score, roc_auc_score cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) models = { "Baseline (majority)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"), "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced"), "Decision tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"), "Random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8, random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"), "Gradient boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0), } rows = [] for name, clf in models.items(): pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prepare), ("clf", clf)]) cv_auc = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc") pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) pred = pipe.predict(X_test) proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] if hasattr(clf, "predict_proba") else pred rows.append({ "model": name, "cv_auc": f"{cv_auc.mean():.3f} ± {cv_auc.std():.3f}", "recall": round(recall_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0), 3), "precision": round(precision_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0), 3), "test_auc": round(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), 3), }) print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model cv_auc recall precision test_auc Baseline (majority) 0.500 ± 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.500 Logistic regression 0.736 ± 0.053 0.685 0.180 0.742 Decision tree 0.643 ± 0.031 0.575 0.209 0.671 Random forest 0.683 ± 0.057 0.521 0.225 0.724 Gradient boosting 0.704 ± 0.040 0.014 0.143 0.749 ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 6 — the threshold is where the business requirement is met **Accuracy was never the goal. The goal was: catch 60% of churners while contacting under 30% of customers.** That is a statement about the decision threshold, not the model. ::: {#cell-fig-s16-threshold .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score best = Pipeline([("prep", prepare), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8, random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"))]) best.fit(X_train, y_train) proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] thresholds = np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.025) recalls = [recall_score(y_test, proba >= t, zero_division=0) for t in thresholds] contacts = [(proba >= t).mean() for t in thresholds] plt.plot(thresholds, recalls, label="churners caught (recall)") plt.plot(thresholds, contacts, label="customers contacted") plt.axhline(0.60, color="green", ls="--", lw=1, label="required recall 0.60") plt.axhline(0.30, color="red", ls="--", lw=1, label="contact budget 0.30") plt.xlabel("decision threshold"); plt.legend(fontsize=8) plt.show() ok = [(t, r, c) for t, r, c in zip(thresholds, recalls, contacts) if r >= 0.60 and c <= 0.30] if ok: t, r, c = ok[0] print(f"Requirement MET at threshold {t:.3f}: recall {r:.1%}, contacting {c:.1%}") else: closest = max(zip(thresholds, recalls, contacts), key=lambda z: z[1] if z[2] <= 0.30 else -1) print(f"Requirement NOT met by this model.") print(f"Within the 30% contact budget the best recall is " f"{closest[1]:.1%} at threshold {closest[0]:.3f}.") print("Report this honestly. Either the budget rises or the model improves.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Recall and contact rate against the decision threshold. The shaded band is where both requirements hold.](session-16-open-ended-module-implementation-and-capstone_files/figure-html/fig-s16-threshold-output-1.png){#fig-s16-threshold width=654 height=408} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Requirement NOT met by this model. Within the 30% contact budget the best recall is 58.9% at threshold 0.450. Report this honestly. Either the budget rises or the model improves. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important title="🔓 Report against the requirement, not against 1.0"} "AUC 0.78" is a number. **"Catches 58.9% of churners within a 30% contact budget, against a target of 60%"** is an answer. Only the second tells anyone whether to deploy. **Notice that this worked example does not meet its own target**, and that this is left in rather than tidied away. That is the realistic outcome: a model with a respectable AUC can still fail the requirement the business actually set. The honest report says so and offers the two real options — **raise the contact budget, or improve the model** — instead of quietly switching to a metric that looks better. A project that reports a missed target with the gap measured is worth more than one that reports a good-looking AUC against no target at all. ::: # Part B — Market basket analysis {#sec-s16-b} ## 4. Association rules {#sec-s16-topic-4} **Association rule mining finds things that occur together.** *"People who buy bread and butter also buy jam."* Written as a rule: **{bread, butter} → {jam}**. The left side is the **antecedent**, the right side the **consequent**. **Three numbers judge every rule.** Compute them by hand once and they never confuse you again. | Measure | Question | Formula | |---|---|---| | **Support** | how often does this combination happen at all? | transactions with all items ÷ all transactions | | **Confidence** | when the left side happens, how often does the right? | support(both) ÷ support(left) | | **Lift** | is the right side **more likely** than usual when the left happens? | confidence ÷ support(right) | **Lift is the one that matters:** | Lift | Means | |---|---| | **> 1** | they go together **more** than chance — a real association | | **= 1** | independent — **the rule found nothing** | | **< 1** | they go together **less** than chance | ### Demo 7 — by hand, on ten baskets ::: {#0c30607d .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Ten baskets, one per line, from a real text file. baskets = [set(line.split()) for line in open("datasets/baskets_small.txt").read().strip().split("\n")] n = len(baskets) for i, b in enumerate(baskets, 1): print(f" basket {i:>2}: {sorted(b)}") print() def support(items): items = set(items) return sum(items <= b for b in baskets) / n left, right = {"bread", "butter"}, {"jam"} s_left = support(left) s_right = support(right) s_both = support(left | right) confidence = s_both / s_left lift = confidence / s_right print(f"Rule: {sorted(left)} → {sorted(right)}\n") print(f" support(bread & butter) = {sum(left <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_left:.2f}") print(f" support(jam) = {sum(right <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_right:.2f}") print(f" support(all three together) = {sum((left|right) <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_both:.2f}") print(f"\n confidence = {s_both:.2f} / {s_left:.2f} = {confidence:.2f}") print(f" → when someone buys bread and butter, {confidence:.0%} of the time they buy jam") print(f"\n lift = {confidence:.2f} / {s_right:.2f} = {lift:.2f}") print(f" → they are {lift:.2f}× more likely to buy jam than a random shopper") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` basket 1: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam'] basket 2: ['bread', 'butter'] basket 3: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam', 'milk'] basket 4: ['eggs', 'milk'] basket 5: ['bread', 'jam'] basket 6: ['bread', 'butter', 'milk'] basket 7: ['butter', 'jam'] basket 8: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam'] basket 9: ['bread', 'eggs', 'milk'] basket 10: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam'] Rule: ['bread', 'butter'] → ['jam'] support(bread & butter) = 6/10 = 0.60 support(jam) = 6/10 = 0.60 support(all three together) = 4/10 = 0.40 confidence = 0.40 / 0.60 = 0.67 → when someone buys bread and butter, 67% of the time they buy jam lift = 0.67 / 0.60 = 1.11 → they are 1.11× more likely to buy jam than a random shopper ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 8 — the trap: high confidence, no information ::: {#ea0f7016 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # A rule about something almost everyone buys. left2, right2 = {"milk"}, {"bread"} c2 = support(left2 | right2) / support(left2) l2 = c2 / support(right2) print(f"Rule: milk → bread") print(f" confidence = {c2:.2f} ← looks impressive") print(f" support(bread) = {support(right2):.2f} ← but bread is in most baskets anyway") print(f" lift = {l2:.2f}") print(f"\n Lift near or below 1 means buying milk tells you NOTHING extra about bread.") print(f" A recommendation engine built on this rule would suggest bread to everybody.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rule: milk → bread confidence = 0.75 ← looks impressive support(bread) = 0.80 ← but bread is in most baskets anyway lift = 0.94 Lift near or below 1 means buying milk tells you NOTHING extra about bread. A recommendation engine built on this rule would suggest bread to everybody. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Confidence alone will fool you"} Any rule pointing at a very common item gets high confidence automatically. **Always check lift**, and be suspicious of any rule whose consequent is your best-selling product. ::: ## 5. Apriori on real-sized data {#sec-s16-topic-5} **Checking every possible combination is impossible** — 100 products give more than 10³⁰ possible itemsets. **Apriori** avoids that with one observation: *if {bread, butter} is rare, then {bread, butter, jam} must be rarer still*, so whole branches can be discarded without checking. ### Demo 9 — mining rules with mlxtend ::: {#d9eca089 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules # 4,000 real baskets. Three rules were planted when the file was generated, # so we can check the algorithm against a truth we know — see # datasets/make_session_16.py. raw = pd.read_csv("datasets/grocery_baskets.csv") transactions = [set(items.split(",")) for items in raw["items"]] products = sorted({p for t in transactions for p in t}) print(f"{len(transactions):,} baskets, {len(products)} distinct products\n") onehot = pd.DataFrame([{p: (p in t) for p in products} for t in transactions]) frequent = apriori(onehot, min_support=0.05, use_colnames=True) # Deliberately NO lift floor here, so we can see how many worthless rules # a permissive search produces. rules = association_rules(frequent, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.10) rules = rules.sort_values("lift", ascending=False) print(f"{len(transactions):,} baskets → {len(frequent)} frequent itemsets → {len(rules)} rules\n") out = rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift"]].head(8).copy() out["antecedents"] = out["antecedents"].apply(lambda s: ", ".join(sorted(s))) out["consequents"] = out["consequents"].apply(lambda s: ", ".join(sorted(s))) print(out.round(3).to_string(index=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4,000 baskets, 10 distinct products 4,000 baskets → 34 frequent itemsets → 56 rules antecedents consequents support confidence lift butter bread, jam 0.116 0.346 2.885 bread, jam butter 0.116 0.967 2.885 butter bread 0.171 0.510 2.483 bread butter 0.171 0.832 2.483 butter, jam bread 0.116 0.487 2.375 bread butter, jam 0.116 0.564 2.375 coffee sugar 0.154 0.779 2.366 sugar coffee 0.154 0.468 2.366 ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 10 — did it find the rules we planted? ::: {#03eef43d .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} planted = [({"bread"}, {"butter"}), ({"butter"}, {"jam"}), ({"coffee"}, {"sugar"})] print("Checking the algorithm against the truth we built in:\n") for ante, cons in planted: hit = rules[(rules["antecedents"] == frozenset(ante)) & (rules["consequents"] == frozenset(cons))] if len(hit): r = hit.iloc[0] print(f" FOUND {sorted(ante)} → {sorted(cons)} " f"confidence {r['confidence']:.2f} lift {r['lift']:.2f}") else: print(f" MISSED {sorted(ante)} → {sorted(cons)}") useless = rules[rules["lift"] < 1.1] print(f"\n{len(useless)} of {len(rules)} rules have lift below 1.1 — they tell you") print("nothing, however good their confidence looks.") if len(useless): worst = useless.sort_values("confidence", ascending=False).iloc[0] print(f" worst offender: {sorted(worst['antecedents'])} → {sorted(worst['consequents'])}") print(f" confidence {worst['confidence']:.2f}, but lift {worst['lift']:.2f} — below 1, so buying") print(f" the antecedent makes the consequent LESS likely than for a random shopper") print("\nFilter on lift FIRST, then read the survivors.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Checking the algorithm against the truth we built in: FOUND ['bread'] → ['butter'] confidence 0.83 lift 2.48 FOUND ['butter'] → ['jam'] confidence 0.71 lift 1.85 FOUND ['coffee'] → ['sugar'] confidence 0.78 lift 2.37 38 of 56 rules have lift below 1.1 — they tell you nothing, however good their confidence looks. worst offender: ['eggs'] → ['jam'] confidence 0.32, but lift 0.83 — below 1, so buying the antecedent makes the consequent LESS likely than for a random shopper Filter on lift FIRST, then read the survivors. ``` ::: ::: # Part C — Making claims stand up {#sec-s16-c} ## 6. Test the claim, do not just draw it {#sec-s16-topic-6} **A box plot showing two groups apart is a hypothesis, not a finding.** The gap might be sampling noise. A statistical test puts a number on how likely that is. | Question | Test | |---|---| | Do two groups differ in a **number**? | **t-test** | | Are two **categories** related? | **chi-square** | | Do three or more groups differ? | **ANOVA** | **The p-value is the probability of seeing a gap this large if there were genuinely no difference.** Small p-value → the gap is unlikely to be chance. ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ What a p-value does not mean"} It is **not** the probability that your hypothesis is true. It is **not** a measure of how big or important the effect is — with 100,000 rows, a trivial difference produces a tiny p-value. **Always report the effect size next to the p-value.** "Churners make 1.4 more support calls on average (p < 0.001)" is a finding. "p < 0.001" alone is not. ::: ### Demo 11 — testing the three hypotheses from Demo 3 ::: {#f4045827 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scipy import stats import pandas as pd churned = clean_df[clean_df["churned"] == 1] retained = clean_df[clean_df["churned"] == 0] print("t-tests: do churners and retained customers differ?\n") for col in ["support_calls", "tenure_months", "monthly_spend"]: t, p = stats.ttest_ind(churned[col], retained[col], equal_var=False) diff = churned[col].mean() - retained[col].mean() # Cohen's d — how big the difference is, in standard deviations pooled = ((churned[col].std()**2 + retained[col].std()**2) / 2) ** 0.5 d = diff / pooled verdict = "REAL" if p < 0.05 else "not significant" size = "large" if abs(d) > .8 else "medium" if abs(d) > .5 else "small" if abs(d) > .2 else "negligible" print(f" {col:<16} difference {diff:>+8.2f} p = {p:<10.2e} {verdict:<16} effect: {size} (d={d:+.2f})") # chi-square: is churn related to the plan a customer is on? table = pd.crosstab(clean_df["plan"], clean_df["churned"]) chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table) print(f"\nchi-square, plan vs churn: χ² = {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.2e}") print(f" → plan and churn are {'related' if p < 0.05 else 'independent'}") print(table.to_string()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` t-tests: do churners and retained customers differ? support_calls difference +0.66 p = 6.67e-16 REAL effect: medium (d=+0.56) tenure_months difference -11.54 p = 4.02e-20 REAL effect: medium (d=-0.59) monthly_spend difference -35.60 p = 2.85e-01 not significant effect: negligible (d=-0.06) chi-square, plan vs churn: χ² = 38.0, p = 5.72e-09 → plan and churn are related churned 0 1 plan basic 1125 176 premium 580 39 standard 1003 77 ``` ::: ::: **Compare this with Demo 3's pictures.** The eye suggested three drivers; the tests confirm which are real, and — importantly — how large each effect actually is. ### Demo 12 — what the model learned, checked against the tests ::: {#5d04e40d .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier rf = Pipeline([("prep", prepare), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8, random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"))]) rf.fit(X_train, y_train) names = rf.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out() importance = pd.Series(rf.named_steps["clf"].feature_importances_, index=names) print("What the model relies on most:") print(importance.sort_values(ascending=False).head(6).round(3).to_string()) print("\nThe top features match the statistically significant ones. When they do NOT,") print("something is wrong — usually a leaked column or a proxy for the target.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` What the model relies on most: num__tenure_months 0.361 num__monthly_spend 0.260 num__support_calls 0.210 cat__plan_basic 0.048 cat__city_Chennai 0.023 cat__plan_standard 0.021 The top features match the statistically significant ones. When they do NOT, something is wrong — usually a leaked column or a proxy for the target. ``` ::: ::: # Part D — Delivering it {#sec-s16-d} ## 7. What you hand over {#sec-s16-topic-7} | Deliverable | Must contain | |---|---| | **Repository** | code that runs from a clean clone, `requirements.txt` with versions pinned, a seed everywhere | | **Report** | the question, what you did, what you found, **and what you could not conclude** | | **Model bundle** | the full pipeline plus its metadata (Session 12) | | **Application** | a deployed link a stranger can open | | **Presentation** | eight minutes: problem, approach, result, limitations | ### Demo 13 — packaging the result (Session 12) ::: {#c35c84f0 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import joblib, sklearn, tempfile, os, json import numpy as np from datetime import date from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score, roc_auc_score folder = tempfile.mkdtemp() path = os.path.join(folder, "churn_model.joblib") proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] thresholds = np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.025) viable = [(t, recall_score(y_test, proba >= t), (proba >= t).mean()) for t in thresholds if (proba >= t).mean() <= 0.30] chosen_t, chosen_recall, chosen_contact = max(viable, key=lambda z: z[1]) bundle = { "pipeline": best, "features": features, "decision_threshold": round(float(chosen_t), 3), "trained_on": str(date.today()), "n_training_rows": int(len(X_train)), "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__, "test_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)), 3), "recall_at_threshold": round(float(chosen_recall), 3), "contact_rate_at_threshold": round(float(chosen_contact), 3), "target_recall": 0.60, "contact_budget": 0.30, "known_limitations": [ "trained on 12 months only; no seasonal effects captured", "support_calls is recorded after a complaint, so very recent calls may be missing", "no data on competitor pricing, which is likely a real driver", ], } joblib.dump(bundle, path) loaded = joblib.load(path) print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in loaded.items() if k != "pipeline"}, indent=2)) print(f"\nmet the target? Responsible delivery {#sec-s16-topic-8} **Before a model touches a real person, answer three questions in writing.** | Question | For this project | |---|---| | **Who could be harmed by a wrong prediction?** | a loyal customer wrongly flagged gets an unnecessary discount — cheap. A churner missed is a lost customer — the expensive error, which is why recall was the target. | | **Does it treat groups differently?** | check the error rate per city and per plan, not just overall | | **Would you be comfortable explaining a decision to the person it affected?** | if the answer needs "component 1 was low", reconsider (Session 6) | ### Demo 14 — a fairness check ::: {#8b4e29b3 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score check = X_test.copy() check["actual"] = y_test.values check["predicted"] = (best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] >= chosen_t).astype(int) print("Does the model perform equally across groups?\n") for group in ["city", "plan"]: print(f"By {group}:") for value, sub in check.groupby(group): if sub["actual"].sum() == 0: continue print(f" {value:<10} n={len(sub):>4} " f"recall {recall_score(sub['actual'], sub['predicted'], zero_division=0):.2f} " f"contacted {sub['predicted'].mean():.1%}") print() recalls = [recall_score(s["actual"], s["predicted"], zero_division=0) for _, s in check.groupby("city") if s["actual"].sum() > 0] print(f"Recall ranges from {min(recalls):.2f} to {max(recalls):.2f} across cities.") print("A large gap means the model serves some groups better than others —") print("worth investigating before anyone acts on it.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Does the model perform equally across groups? Write the four answers from Demo 1: the decision, the success criterion **with a number**, the data available, and what would make the model useless. **Fix these before writing code.** **Task 2 — Clean and explore.** Produce a cleaning report and an EDA section that ends with three written hypotheses. **Task 3 — Test the hypotheses.** For each, run the appropriate test and report the p-value **and** the effect size. Say which survived. **Task 4 — Model.** Compare at least four models against a baseline, cross-validated with the spread reported. Tune the best one without touching the test set. **Task 5 — Meet the requirement.** Choose the decision threshold that satisfies your Task 1 criterion, **or report honestly that no threshold does.** **Task 6 — Mine the rules.** If your data has transactions, run Apriori and report the three most useful rules by lift. Explain why each is actionable. **Task 7 — Deliver.** Bundle the pipeline with metadata and limitations, deploy a Streamlit app, and write the report. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="✅ A capstone that passes"} - [ ] Runs from a clean clone, first try, with versions pinned - [ ] States a success criterion that was fixed **before** the modelling - [ ] Beats a named baseline, with the baseline's score printed - [ ] Reports at least one thing that was tried and did not work - [ ] Supports every claim with a test **and** an effect size, not just a chart - [ ] Has a deployed link a stranger can open - [ ] Names who could be harmed by a wrong prediction, and checks group fairness - [ ] **Says clearly what the result cannot support** ::: # ❓ MCQs {#sec-s16-mcqs} **Q1.** A rule has confidence 0.85 and lift 1.02. Is it useful? - (a) Yes, 85% confidence is high. - (b) **No — lift near 1 means the consequent is no more likely than usual.** - (c) Only if support is high. **Q2.** Why fix the success criterion before modelling? - (a) It is required by scikit-learn. - (b) **Otherwise you choose the metric your model happens to do well on.** - (c) It speeds up training. **Q3.** Your t-test gives p = 0.0001 and Cohen's d = 0.04. What do you report? - (a) A highly significant, important finding. - (b) **A real but negligibly small difference — significant because the sample is large, not because it matters.** - (c) Nothing; the p-value is too small. **Q4.** The model's most important feature is one the statistical tests found insignificant. What should you suspect? - (a) The tests were wrong. - (b) **Leakage, or a proxy for the target — investigate that column.** - (c) Nothing; models see things tests cannot. **Q5.** What is the most valuable section of a project report? - (a) The accuracy figure. - (b) The code listing. - (c) **What the result cannot support, and why.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A1 — (b).** Demo 8 measured exactly this case. **A2 — (b).** The criterion is a commitment; chosen afterwards it is a rationalisation. **A3 — (b).** With enough rows any difference becomes significant. The effect size is what says whether anyone should care. **A4 — (b).** Demo 12's closing note. This mismatch is one of the most reliable leakage detectors there is. **A5 — (c).** It is what lets somebody else use the result safely — and it is the section that is almost always missing. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you finish the course"} Sixteen chapters, one sentence each: 1. Data science turns recorded facts into decisions 2. Get data in with pandas; look before you touch 3. Clean in order — duplicates, impossible, missing, noise, outliers, text 4. Join carefully, and check the row count every time 5. Split before you scale; encode text; never leak 6. Fewer columns is often better; say what the reduction cost 7. Report a centre **and** a spread **and** a shape 8. Every chart answers a question you asked first 9. A model is a rule learned from examples; beat a baseline 10. Clustering has no answer key — justify the result instead 11. One split is one opinion; cross-validate and report the spread 12. Save the pipeline, validate inputs, watch for drift 13. Big data is a symptom, not a size; try chunking first 14. Map, shuffle, reduce — and the shuffle is the expensive part 15. NoSQL trades schema for flexibility; aggregate in the database 16.
